passages.title: Private houses expose the delay in a shared task
passages.summary: In the second year of Darius, Haggai speaks to the governor and the high priest. The people say it is not yet time to rebuild the LORD’s house. God asks whether they should live in paneled houses while his house lies ruined. They sow much and harvest little. Their wages go into a bag with holes. God tells them to bring wood and build. The leaders and the people obey. Within a month the work begins.
passages.uncertainty: Jerusalem marks the rebuilding setting. The mountain supplying wood is unnamed and receives no route.

lds.text: The lesson connects considering one’s ways with giving temple work higher priority. Why does Haggai compare private houses with God’s ruined house?

contextNote.title: Private houses expose the delay in a shared task
contextNote.text: Verse 4 notes that the people’s own houses are finished and paneled. Verse 9 says each one “is busy with his own house.” The trouble is where their energy goes. Haggai reads their poor harvests as a signal to stop and think. The response is quick. Verses 1 and 15 are dated twenty-three days apart. Ezra 5:1–2 records the same new start.

passages.title: The smaller building does not end God's presence
passages.summary: A month later Haggai speaks again. He asks who remembers the first temple in its glory. The new one looks like nothing beside it. Yet God tells the governor, the priest, and the people to be strong and work. He is with them, and his Spirit remains among them. He will shake the nations and fill this house with glory. From the day the foundation was laid, he will bless them. He tells the governor that he has chosen him.
passages.uncertainty: Jerusalem marks the rebuilding setting. Egypt is a remembered regional reference, not a present journey.

lds.text: The lesson compares encouragement for the builders with later Church teaching about temples. Why does the promise of presence matter before greater glory or a new harvest?

contextNote.title: The smaller building does not end God's presence
contextNote.text: Verse 3 says honestly that the new building looks like nothing. Ezra 3:12 shows old men weeping at the sight. Verse 4 does not deny the difference. It says “be strong” three times and then “work.” The reason is God’s presence, not the size of the house. Verse 5 ties that presence to the exodus. Glory is promised for later (verse 9), and the work is for now.
